On the motion for Committee of Supply:

Before the House resolves itself into Committee of Supply, as intimated previously, I am taking occasion to say a few words with reference to questions involving transportation rates, control of rates and such like, which were discussed while the Estimates of the department were under consideration. In the remarks that I propose making I shall try to look at all sides of these knotty and troublesome questions which have been
. 
thrust upon us largely by conditions arising from the war. I am going to make what little contribution I can make to a discussion of these points, with the idea of interesting the House and of provoking suggestions and opinions which will tend to explain if not to solve the conditions under which we are labouring.
In the discussion of these matters by gentlemen on the other side of the House/ the Government has been held responsible for several things. Mainly it has been held responsible for the increase of freight rates across the Atlantic, for scarcity of tonnage for Atlantic transport, and for utter neglect or negligence in respect of both these matters. Although most of the members of this House may be thoroughly conversant with what I shall bring out this afternoon, and may, therefore, look upon it as being an iteration of what is already known, I am convinced that	such is not the	case
amongst the people at large. These questions with reference to freight rates, control of freight rates, and transport across the Atlantic are not easily understood by the majority of the people, and consequently, in view of the statements that have been made as to what the Government has not done, there may easily be raised in their minds the presumption that things could have been very different from what they are if the Government had taken an active interest in these matters or had been possessed of capacity to deal with them. A good deal of this will probably be old matter to many of you who sit in the Chamber this afternoon; but I am addressing my remarks not only to the members of the House, but to the public outside, in the hope that a little more light may be thrown upon the matters under consideration.
The scarcity of tonnage is the key to the whole situation. Rates have advanced because of the scarcity of tonnage, and they have advanced in proportion as this scarcity of tonnage has become more pronounced. The \ lack of transport and the control of rates is connected with the general transport of our products overseas. How has this scarcity of tonnage which, as I say, is the key to the whole position, been brought about? In the first place, the commercial marine of the world has been sadly confused and hardly dealt with. The mercantile marine which belonged to the Teutonic nations has been absolutely swept from the seas. A

large proportion of it has been kept in home ports, mainly in Germany and in Austria; a large proportion of it has been interned in neutral ports where it happened to be when the war broke out or where it happened to find refuge shortly after the outbreak of war in order to avoid capture. When you put these two elements together you account for the disappearance of a very large proportion of the commercial tonnage of the world-tonnage which was absolutely and immediately abstracted from carrying capacity and power. Then, too, there has been the destruction of enemy tonnage through the activities of the war. Ships have been sent to the bottom; ships have been destroyed in different ways. When you take this into account you have one great factor accounting for the scarcity of tonnage Which has been felt all over the world; because this commercial tonnage of the Teutonic nations went everywhere and was not confined to any one or two routes. These had been so developed by Germany during the last fifteen or twenty years that German lines of communication extended to every quarter of the world.
The next factor in producing scarcity of tonnage is the weight of work that has to be performed by the commercial marine of the allied powers and of the neutral nations, in supporting the active operations of the war. The transports and naval vessels of the allied powers have been engaged in the transport of troops and munitions from the bases of supply to the fields of action, many of them in taking care of that ceaseless stream of war traffic between Great Britain and France, and a large portion of them in caring for those distant operation which are being carried on in every part of the world by the British and allied nations. These operations have been conducted on an extensive scale in the Mediterranean, in the far East and in South Africa, and they have made a very great demand on commercial tonnage. In proportion as the war ha3 extended and has developed in intensity and in the numbers of men engaged, particularly on the part of the British Empire, the naval transports have proved unequal to the added work and the call upon the British commercial marine has been accentu-ate.d and made greater, month by month, and year by year. Supplies and troops have had to be transported to the scene of the war from far distant countries,-New Zeafand, Australia, South Africa, and the 199
dependencies of Great Britain all over the world. Owing to the great length of the voyages in such cases the demand upon the mercantile marine is very much greater than where the troops and supplies have to be transported only a short distance. No one, without actual investigation, can comprehend the amount of commercial tonnage that has been required to carry out this work. Not only have multiplied munitions of war had to 'be carried from far distant countries, very largely from the United States, but it has been necessary to provide transportation for immense quantities of supplies, food, provisions of all kinds and great numbers of horses and mules. It must also be remembered that Great Britain has had to look after not only her own wants but she has had to supply commercial tonnage for France, Italy, and other Allies. So, when we sometimes feel almost like finding fault because Great Britain requisitions ships which are engaged in mercantile operations, we must take into account not only the vast needs of Great Britain for her own purppses but also that she has to supply commercial tonnage to a very large extent for the war purposes of her Allies.
It must be remembered, also, that at all times during the war, and particularly of late, there has been a certain destruction of tonnage by the enemy. It would surprise any member of this House if he were to total up the quantity of commercial tonnage which has been destroyed by mines within the two years of the war, and, of late, by enemy submarines. Outside of all accidents and casualties common to the sea there have been these influences which have taxed to the utmost the commercial tonnage, not only of Great Britain, but of the neutral countries as well. Coincident with the destruction and internment of tonnage there has been going on in Great Britain and in the allied countries a certain amount of shipbuilding. It would not be far from the truth to say that the tonnage built for commercial purposes since the war began has been sufficient to offset the destruction by mines and submarines, and by casualties, and even with, perhaps, a slight surplus up to within a very recent period. I think the truth is that just now the new shipbuilding from month to month will hardly replace the actual destruction of tonnage by warlike operations.
Added to that destruction of tonnage there has been a demand for the carrying of products unprecedented, possibly, in the

Now, when we have these three vessels with a combined carrying capacity of 15,000 tons, we have Canadian shippers and producers with hundreds of thousands of tons of produce to be shipped. To which one of those shippers will you allocate those vessels at a low rate of freight? You cannot discriminate. The wheat man wants the wheat carried; the lobster man wants the lobsters carried; the cheese man wants the cheese carried; the manufacturers want their products carried, and so on with the asbestos man and the paper man: all have equal rights to be considered. How are you going to discriminate between the lines of goods you will carry at a lower rate, and provide no tonnage for other lines at a like rate? How are you to discriminate between the parties who own the line of goods you decide to carry? Take wheat, fot instance. You have a carrying capacity of 15,000 tons. To what wheat shippers will you go and say: here is a chance for you to get 5,000 tons of freight carried at a lower rate than you can get it carried by another ship. You would discriminate in favour of one and against others in that way. Your only refuge is to maintain the normal rate, and let your ships carry all that you can possibly pack into them at that rate, so that no one will be discriminated against. I do not see any Gther way Out of it. That faced me immediately I went into the market to attempt to charter vessels. I could not accede to the demand that in chartering a vessel I should bring the rate down, because then I should be faced with this problem who is it that you are going to favour and carry his goods at a lower rate, while hundreds of other men about him cannot get a chance on your ship at that lower rate? That was the difficulty and it was impossible to face it successfully on any other ground than this: that you charge the current normal rate, and let whoever might be able take advantage of that much space on your ship. That is the position that I think some of us fail to take into account when we ask the Government to charter vessels to bring down the rate, and engage, so far as we possibly can, in the carrying of what, after all, would be an infinitesimally small proportion of the freight offering. The very same difficulty is met in the purchase of vessels. There seems to be no escape from the position that, if you are to help out in this emergency by purchas-
ing or chartering vessels, you can do it under present conditions only by charging the current rates; and if you are to submit to that condition, then somebody else might just as well charter those vessels and put them on the route as the Government. Nothing is gained in the matter of carriage capacity, nothing is gained in the matter of rates. The Government did face that difficulty, and did make very serious and general inquiries into the possibility of chartering vessels; but it was met with these conditions, which made it difficult for the Government to alct beneficially. And, what was the necessity of incurring responsibility unless some good could accrue?
Leaving that branch of the subject for a moment, one very marked criticism has been made-I have seen it thousands of times, in the papers, in platform speeches, and I think it has been made in this House by members on either one or the other side -and it is this:	A man in The West today sells his grain-taking grain as an illustration-in Winnipeg at a dollar, we. will say; it can be sold for more than a dollar, but we will take that figure. The statement is made that he has to pay 45 cents for the' grain to cross the ocean, plus whatever it takes to get the grain from Winnipeg to the ocean, which we will assume to be 20 cents. There is 20 and 45 cents that the man has to encounter before his bushel of grain can be delivered at Liverpool, and the statement is very commonly made that but for these iniquitous rates the western farmer would get very much more for his wheat at Winnipeg; that is, he would get. the difference between the old transporation rate and the present rate, which would be in the neighbourhood of 45 cents per bushel.
The argument is made and the lesson is sought to be taught that on account of those high freight rates the western farmer gets that much less for his wheat, and that if the ocean rate were brought down from 45 cents to 10 cents, the western farmer would have the difference of 35 cents to put in his pocket. My hon. friend (Mr. Turriff), who is looking at me, may be guilty of having used that argument himself; he smiles as though he were; but if he is not guilty of it, many people are, and I could almost vouch, if he heard any one putting forward that argument in the West, he would not sweat very much in an endeavour to get him away from that argument. On the other side, in Liverpool you have the

man who wants the bushel of grain. He says:	Grain is so much at normal value
in Winnipeg; but I have to pay 65 cents on that bushel to get it to Liverpool; if that rate were reduced 45 cents, I would have the difference to put in my pocket because I would pay that much less for the bushel of grain when it was delivered to me at Liverpool. Now, you cannot have the thing both ways. My own opinion expressed before the House to-day is that it is a case in which the consumer pays, if not every red cent of it, almost every red cent of it. We have an offer for the building of steel vessels, and the general terms of that offer I will state to the House. Two steel vessels could have been built for this Dominion Government at a rate of $125 to $135 per ton, with delivery in the middle part of the year 1917. That is the best offer we got for steel tonnage. The amount asked for, of course, is very large; but the time of delivery is also a factor in the case which must be considered. What we must do in Canada is to divide this thing into two. There is a period of emergency, and there will be a period to succeed this emergency. Having canvassed, to a certain extent, the emergency period, let me now say a few words with reference to the work of shipbuilding in Canada on the basis of permanency, that is, with reference not to the present emergency but	to
the conditions and the needs of	the
future. It goes without saying, to my mind, that a country of such large productive capacity as Canada, and with production constantly increasing, occupies an undesirable position if it does not produce and have at command a very considerable commercial tonnage for its own use. That becomes apparent in times like this when, with no commercial marine, the country is at the mercy of the disturbing conditions of war. Altogether, it is a fair axiom that a country with the producing capacity of Canada ought to have a reasonable and growing mercantile marine; and I believe that Canada can have it. It ought to have it, for these potential reasons; it ought to have it because commercial tonnage taken year in and year out, is a profitable investment for a country. Great Britain's wealth is largely built up on. the earnings of her commercial marine. Holland, and formerly Belgium, are notable examples of the wealth that comes to countries from large commercial marine, employed year in and year out, having their periods of prosperity and their corresponding periods of adversity, but bringing on the average a good return to the country in earning power. Canada as well ought to try in some way or other to build up a good commercial marine. How is it possible to do that? One may say: let capital run its own course; if capital sees that it would be profitable to invest in building commercial tonnage for Canada, it will do it; on the other hand, if it cannot see its way clear to do that; if it feels that it should depend upon the carrying capacity of outside vessels, it will take its chance in the open market of the world and charter or procure its tonnage as it has necessity for it. I believe that this argument should go along the line of a country having a good, strong, commercial marine of its own, and I do not think you can bring that about by leaving the matter entirely to corporate and private enterprise without some form of aid. Now, what are the forms of aid which can be given? There is a tonnage construction subsidy, whereby for every ton of capacity of vessels built in Canada under certain conditions the Government-the Treasury, the people generally might pay a certain amount in order to give an impetus, at least in its early stages, to the building of a commercial marine. That is one method that can be employed, and it has its disadvantages. In the first place, a vessel that you subsidize by tonnage construction subsidy may be in your employ a year after the vessel is built or it may be sold and be in some one else's employ -thereafter. This is liable to happen unless you hedge the subsidy around with conditions requiring that the vessel shall make itself available for Canadian trade, and that stipulation is difficult to append to a simple tonnage subsidy agreement.
There is a scheme which, has been adopted and which has in it, I think, a good deal of merit; I am going to give the outlines of it this afternoon, but I shall first call attention to what the United States Government is now proposing. Hast year a Bill was introduced in the United States Congress for the promotion of shipbuilding in the United States. This year the Bill has been modified, and the lines of the present Bill, which has the administration behind it, and is being pressed in the United States, are something of this kind: an appropriation of $50,000,000 is to be made and

secured upon Panama canal bonds; that $50,000,000 so secured is placed in the hands of a committee, or commission, consisting. of certain members of' the United States Cabinet, a naval architect and other persons chosen by the President, with the assent of the Senate, and these men so selected are to be thoroughly conversant with shipping matters and shipbuilding. This governmental commission is in charge of shipbuilding under this scheme. It says what kind of vessels shall be built, how they shall be built and their tonnage, and it has general direction over such matters. The shipbuilding which is carried on under this scheme-and this includes purchases of vessels-is subject to these conditions. This commission shall have charge of shipping matters so far as they relate to that proposition, and they have also the right to license vessels trading to the United States and to control rates as far as possible. That $50,000,000 being at their disposal, they may enter into contract with parties to build or purchase vessels in the United States, and to purchase vessels outside of the United States, these vessels to be placed upon the United States register of tonnage and to become United States vessels. Entering into contract with' these parties for the purchase or building of ships, the commission is empowered to subscribe stock to these ships, in building or in purchase, taking care always to have a majority of the stock so as to enable them to keep the control. On that basis the whole proposition, outside of the financial aid which is given, looks at the acquisition by the United States-by building in and out of the United States and by purchase out of the United States-of vessels'on certain standard lines, which vessels shall be built or purchased and operated under the regulations of this commission. They have also in the United States a mail contract law, by which vessels of twenty knots and upwards get $4 per mile on approved routes for carrying the mail, while vessels of sixteen to twenty knots get $2 a mile. These are the propositions which are to-day before the United States 'Congress looking to the upbuilding of a commercial marine in that country.
The Chamber of Commerce in New York, which is a very influential body, has criticised that scheme, and has put forward another scheme. I purpose giving that scheme in brief to the House this afternoon, and in order to bring it down directly

to ourselves I will translate it into the form.it would take if it were applied to the Dominion of Canada. Applying to Canada that scheme, which was debated and unanimously approved by the New York Chamber of Commerce, it would work out something like this: You would appoint in the Dominion of Canada a commission consisting, we will say, of three members of the Cabinet whose departments aTe interested-for instance, Commerce, Navy, and Finance. The Government side of that commission would be the ministers of these three departments. Add to these a naval instructor and three practical and experienced men in shipping matters, selected by the Government, and you have the commission which would operate in Canada. That commission would have general oversight and direction of the classes of vessels to be built under the scheme; how they should be standardized, how they should be manned, everything in connection with them, and, to the extent that it would be possible, the regulation of the rates as well. That committee would then be empowered to enter into contracts with shipbuilding companies, , to build according to the plans and regulations laid down in Canadian shipyards, and the builders of the ships would be allowed the difference between the cost of construction in Canada and in European ports, that difference having been carefully ascertained by the commission. The object would be to enable the Canadian shipowner to have his ships built in Canada with exactly the same cost to himself as if he had them built in a European port. If the tonnage could be built in a European port at a certain percentage per ton cheaper than in Canada, then the subsidy for construction'would be that difference in cost, whatever it was, so as to put the Canadian shipowner on an equality, in the after competition, with his competitor who had ships built in European snipyards. The time during which this should be carried out would be limited to a period of say 10 years, so that during that 10 years this operation of building would go on. Then the commission would be empowered to enter into contracts with the ship owners, when the ships were built, and to guarantee to the owners the difference in cost of operating'the ships under the Canadian flag and under a European flag, that subsidy to continue for the life of the ship. The commission would possess itself of accurate information on the difference both in cost of construction and in cost of operation, and would pay that

difference, and that difference alone. In that connection we should place at the disposal of the Commission the sum of $15,000,000 or $20,000,000, and empower that commission to guarantee the bonds upon the ships built up to 50 per cent of the value of the ships. Such bonds would be 5 per cent bonds, and the Government Commission would get one-half of one per cent on those bonds returned to its treasury for its work and its supervision.
What would that mean? It would mean that for 10 years you would have shipbuilding tried out under the advantage of a bonus equal to the difference in construction cost in Canada and the difference of operation cost; the latter subvention to extend to the life of the ship. Capital would be attracted and induced to invest in steamships owing to the Government guarantee of bonds, which would, of course, be given under a proper amortization scheme by which those bonds would be provided for and paid off during a certain period.
On the Great Lakes you will find a very large and prosperous American mercantile marine, and I am told that almost every vessel in that fleet has been built under a guarantee of bonds, not a guarantee by the Government, either state or federal, but on that same system; and I am informed that those bonds are considered so good a security that banks, including savings banks, are anxious to get them, and that, in the late history, at least, of those transactions, there has not been an instance of failure with reference to the amortization of the bonds or to the security in any way. But we must recollect that lake marine business is a very different thing from ocean tonnage business. However, that is simply an illustration of what has been done along that line.
Let us see what would be the advantage to be obtained if that system were carried out? In the first place, the Government would make its equitable, yearly contributions, not on a supposed or an imaginary or a favoured basis, but on the actual difference of cost of construction and operation. And, in the next place, it would guarantee bonds of the ship to one-half its value, getting	back	one-half of one
per cent, with arrangements for proper amortization. If you take the history *of lake shipping, there is fair ground for stating that system that would work out satisfactorily and successfully. It is impossible to say what the subsidy would amount to in actual figures; the only
certainty we would have being that it would amount to the actual difference and to ni more and no less. In that way, if it worked out successfully, at the end of 10 years you would have a very substantial commercial ocean marine and you would have the certainty of its operation for 20 years from the time that each steamship went into actual service. By such a plan capital would be attracted to that kind of investment, to which our people in Canada are not very much used; and if you could bring it about that capital would become interested, as construction went on capital would more and more come in, so that the private capital of the country, without Government aid, would afterwards be able to look after its commercial marine. You would have a valuable earning power, proportionate to the amount of tonnage, which would accrue to the people of this country. Our people would have the advantage of the expenditure of money for wages and materials in connection with these ships, and I am assured that if such a policy, based on permanent conditions, were inaugurated in this country, Canada would make the steel necessary for the building of those steel ships, and that we would thus have the benefit of a further development of the steel industry. We would derive many other advantages, which I shall not take time to enumerate, but which would come from a more or less steady supply of ocean tonnage, somewhat commensurate with the needs of a great producing country, requiring large ocean transportation facilities.

If that amount were spread over fifteen years, it would mean a bonus of $180,000 for a vessel which, at the very highest prices prevailing to-day, would not cost over $120,000; in other words, it would be asking $60,000 more than the cost of the
vessel. We all know very well that at the present time, and probably for a number of years to come, those vessels will be able to earn very large profits, and that is why I stated that the suggestion which was apparently made to the Minister of Trade and Commerce was a most 5 p.m. unreasonable one, and that if this Government were bona fide in putting before the people of this country the idea that they were willing to give assistance for the building of wooden ships as well as steel ships, I could not imagine for a single moment that they would not receive much more reasonable offers. Two hundred wooden vessels, with a capacity of
2,000	tons each, would mean a very great addition to the mercantile marine of Canada. Even if you had 100 vessels, that would mean a tonnage of 200,000, and in the course of a year those vessels vould be able to transport from Canada to the markets of the Old Country and to bring back upwards of 2,000,000 tons of produce, which would be a large quantity and would prove of enormous assistance. The total cost of those vessels, if my information is correct, would not exceed $10,000,000; and, in view of the necessity of increasing the production of Canada, and in view also of the necessity of getting a market for that production, and of getting it to that market at a reasonable rate, # would	it be

What we want to do, dt seems to me, is not to look forward to what may be done in five or ten years from now, after the war is over, but to consider what shall be done now to relieve the present necessities. The minister, if I understood him aright, has argued that after all the Canadian producer is not injured very much by the high freight rates. He argues very eloquently that the

farmer gets, Tinder any circumstances, a reasonable price for his grain. I suppose he would argue that the buyer gets a reasonable price, and that the freight on the railway and across the Atlantic is added to the cost to the consumer. My hon. friend may be right as to that, but I do not think so. One might argue as well that, if the milling companies earn enormous profits so that they are able to pay, not only a dividend upon their preferred stock which represents actual capital, but enormous dividends upon their common stock which represents no capital at all, but only water, that does not come out of the wheat producer but out of the people who consume flour. I would rather think it comes out of both the producer and the consumer. If the miller would be content with a less profit, the consumer would pay a less price for the flour and the' former would get a higher price for his wheat. We know that hundreds of the tramp steamers which are upon the Atlantic to-day pay for their cost in two or three voyages, and it seems to me therefore that those extra and unnecessary profits are paid both by the consumer in England or other European countries and by the producer of the grain in 'Canada. If you reduce the rates of freight you are conferring a benefit not merely upon the consumer but upon the Canadian farmer. It does seem to me that the minister is hardly justified in saying that the Canadian producer does not suffer from the increased rates. Take the case of lumber. I do not wish to take up more time than is necessary. Nor do I wish to unduly criticise this Government, for I realize that they have many difficulties to contend with. But I do hold very strongly that they have not given to this question of transportation the care and attention which they ought to have given to it. I do not think the Government is doing credit to itself, nor has it measured up to the responsibility it owes to the people. Let him come down with a scheme for building up a Canadian merchant marine-not, as I have said, for building vessels ten years from now, or five years from now, but at the present day- and he will find support. Mistakes have been made, and, in the end some money may be lost. But the object is so important and the benefits to accrue from increased tonnage operated under the control of the Canadian Government are so great, as, I think, to justify us in running some risk of making mistakes. I say again that if the minister will come down with a matured policy which can be put into operation without unnecessary delay, I for one I cannot speak for others-will be prepared to give that policy my heartiest support. It affords me no pleasure to criticise my hon. friend under present circumstances and in the trying position in which he is placed. But he comes to us with a statement that he gets no sympathy from the members of this House,-he speaks as if he gets no sympathy from his colleagues, as if he were " ploughing his lonely furrow." He turns his back upon his colleagues and in effect says: " I get no sympathy, no support, no encouragement, from the men by whom I am surrounded; " and he looks over to us with an appealing glance in his eye and asks us to stand by him and not only give him support but tell him what he ought to do under these trying circumstances. Let him come down to-morrow with a policy for engaging at once in the building of ships, both steel and wooden, to the number really necessary to meet present conditions and to take the place of the waning ocean merchant marine as far as Canada is concerned, and he will receive from us, even if he does not receive it from his colleagues, earnest consideration and hearty sympathy such as, I am sure', will warm the cockles of his heart. And from many private members on the other side of the House, I am sure, he will receive support and sympathy.

I wish to compliment the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the broad-gauge speech he has made this afternoon on this important question. It is true, his speech is open to criticism in some respects; but in the few minutes I shall occupy I shall not devote myself to criticism so much as to an expression of my delight with the
AP&IlL 26, 1916
way in which the minister has brought this proposition before the House. He has appealed for national consideration of a great national question; he.has appealed to the Opposition and to all the members of the House practically to' go into Committee of the Whole to deal with the transportation question, especially with the question of ocean transportation. The minister made another notable speech this session. I did not happen to be here on that occasion. He made an appeal to this House to do away with the system of patronage, and asked the Opposition and the whole House to take that matter into serious consideration. I think he is proceeding on the right lines. We have had too much party government in this country, and, in view of the present crisis we ought to have more national government iand less party government, and we ought to try to deal with these great problems from a national point of view. I cannot but recall what happened in this House when the Naval Aid Bill was before us. I made, an appeal then to the House, pointing out that the opportunity was then afforded for the two parties to co-operate in working out a system for the defence of the Empire. We were not successful in that; the proposal was practically abandoned at that time. My contention to-day is that, the great problems which this war has created cannot be solved by a single party, and will not be solved unless the House and the country approach them as a nation from a national point of view and irrespective of party. And if you apply this to part of a question you must apply it to the whole question. If the minister asks far the cooperation of the whole House and the whole country in regard to transportation by sea, the same course must be followed in regard to transportation by land. My contention, therefore, is that the only solution of these problems of transportation is the co-operation of both parties in the adoption of a national policy supported by a national Parliament. We cannot deal properly with the railway question now before the country if we deal with them from the party point of view. We are confronted by the most serious problems in connection with railways that we have ever had before us; for the fact that these problems have arisen, both parties may be responsible. If that is the case, we ought to correct our mistakes by dealing with these matters from a non-partisan standpoint. Unless both parties co-operate in
considering these problems, as was pointed out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. to-day, we should not be able to solve them. In the matter of ' transportation both by land and by sea we must arrive at some kind of united policy; the country expects us to deal with these questions from a non-partisan point of view. The member for St. John city made a rather reasonable suggestion to-day, although the method suggested had a tendency to be somewhat partisan. I understood him to intimate that he and his friends were disposed to co-operate in matters of this kind. While not much has been done in the House in the matter of national co-operation concerning these questions, there is a good deal of feeling in the country in favour of that idea. There has been cooperation of parties in the Mother Country with a view of solving the difficulties that have arisen; if they have not quite succeeded over there, I believe that at least they have improved the condition of affairs. None of these questions can be approached and settled in any other way than by some kind of co-operation. Will the question of Civil Service reform in Canada ever be settled by each party in this House putting up the Tecord of the other and pointing out the mistakes of the other in connection with that matter? No; you will arrive at a new and progressive measure only by some kind of co-operation. The remarkable thing about the speech of the minister to-day is not that he did not quite come forward with a substantive policy for dealing with the transportation problem so far as ocean traffic was concerned, so much as it is that he came forward with an appeal to both parties to cooperate in their efforts to deal satisfactorily with the question of shipbuilding. I simply want to content myself with saying to-day that, having regard to the great problems now before us, we should not 'be doing our duty to this country or to the Empire if we do not have this co-operation. Further, if there is to be co-operation in connection with shipbuilding and transportation at sea, there must be co-operation in connection with railways and many other things.
Speaking on broad lines, what is the solution of the transportation problem in Canada? It is that we must have a national policy with regard to railways, which means public ownership of our railways; and we must have a national policy with regard to transportation at sea. To my mind the difficulty will have to be approached by

national1 ownership or national control of ships, very much along the lines outlined by the minister to-day. Great evils havie arisen from the manner in which transportation has been carried on in the past, especially through tbe operations of private monopolies. Private monopolies have taken advantage of the public on every occasion in. the past, and they will do it in the future. A proper national policy supported 'by all the people would build up a transportation system both by land and sea that would seek to serve the public rather than to take advantage of it. The greatest advantage that has ever been taken of the public has been by the shipbuilding and ship owning interests of Great Britain. They have soaked the public right and left in transportation, charges. It has been argued that because these ships were privately owned and operated under a different flag they could not be controlled by Canada. I have never subscribed to that doctrine. I do not agree that we should lie down before them; that we should not seek to control them by some kind of legislation.. That may be an- expensive and roundabout way of doing it, but it is a comparatively easy thing to start a national policy on the line of national ownership, or national control of shipbuilding, and in that way -bring immediate relief to the transportation conditions in this country. As I pointed out in this House when discussing the railway question some time ago, what is the use of our appointing a Railway Commission to regulate railway rates- if we cannot also regulate the charges at sea by the ship monopolies? All the advantages- if there were advantages-accruing to the people from the subsidies- paid in connection with the construction of railways, and from the passing of the Act creating the Railway Commission havie been taken away from them by reason of the fact that the shipbuilding interests have been allowed to charge what they liked in connection with transportation at sea. As a consequence rates were increased not a thousand-fold, as t-he last speaker -said, but to -an amount from four to eight times as high as the rates -that formerly obtained. I do not quite agree with the minister when he says that the consumer paid the larger portion of the increase on these rates. Perhaps what he intimated was that the increase was equally divided between the consumer and the producer. In any case, if we had had- national control of the rates' at sea as well as by land, especially in connection 
with ocean transportation systems, we should be able to give the Canadian producer the bes-t advantage that he possibly could get both by land and by sea-by land especially-and we should be able to give the consumer also the best advantage that he could get. After sixty years of railroad building and experience in matters connected with shipping, the public cannot obtain that measure of advantage to which th-ey are entitled otherwise than by national ownership and national control on new and progressive lines. There has 'been a failure up to date, no matter how much, we have spent in getting improved transportation in this country. The United States, judging by the evidence brought forward this -afternoon, are coming to the idea that they must have a national system of transportation by sea. If they are to have it by sea they must have it also by land. This all goes to show that the trend of public opinion these days is that relief from high transportation charges, whether by land or by sea, must come by national ownership; it will never be attained as long as private control of monopolies prevails on this continent. Owing to the war, England has taken over her railways, and has practically commandeered all the ships -at sea for the service of the public. But the trouble is that the number of ships is rapidly declining o\ying to attacks and destruction at sea, and we do not know when that is going to end. So it is up to the Government and up to the House, in view of this condition of affairs, to inaugurate forthwith some kind of national policy, or party policy if we must have it, looking to the establishment of a great Canadian merchant marine. One reason why I supported the idea of naval aid four years ago was that it would have started a great shipbuilding industry in this country. While it would have been primarily and in the first instance for the building of w.ar ships, it would have ended in the production and the building of a commercial marine. That did not quite come then. It should have been started four years ago, before the war came on. But the war is on now; it is in its second year, and the best judges say to-day that next year will not end it. Then, I say, the_ responsibility is on the Government to' inaugurate forthwith a policy in the direction of encouraging shipbuilding in this country.
Hear, hear.

It must be not only
an encouragement to get the ships built,

but to control them when they are built, and to cons-ecrate them to -the trade of the country and the development of that trade. What is the use of inviting settlers to come to the great Canadian West, to locate there and to develop the land, if the transportation charges are to be so heavy that they will absorb all of the products of the farm except enough to keep the farmer on the land. We are not going to settle our lands, we are not going to get the right people there and to have them develop our country as it should be developed, no matter how much we spend on an immigra-tiorf policy, unless the Government and Parliament, representing the people of this country, control the system of transportation both by land and sea, absolutely. We have tried private ownership of railways now for 60 years and what have we got to show in the way of rates? We have a magnificent service which has been of great benefit to the country. But as regards rates our conditions are not at all what they should be. We have three transcontinental lines, it is true, but for the same amount of money a much better service could have been secured if the transportation question had been handled from a national point of view. We would thus have avoided the duplication of construction and, a still worse evil, the duplication of service. Of the three transcontinental lines now existing there are miles and miles that are mere duplication and which are practically a waste of money. We have the other problem before us and must deal with it, perhaps this session, that is the problem of the unnecessary duplication of service. We have failed in regard to railways, and we will fail in regard to ships unless we have a real national policy, which implies co-operation. I do not care how this great reform is effected. You may say that under our system it must be by party Government. But is party Government to exist forever in this country, after the fruits we have had from it in the past? Is there not a need and a call for some *kind of co-operation? We are asked now for cd-operation in regard to the war, at the most critical point in the world's history. Well, if co-operation is necessary in time of war, are we not to have it in time of peace in regard to trade and transportation, the development and the settlement of the country, and in dealing with financial problems, including banking and currency? I compliment the minister on his speech.
I know it has the weakness that it has not presented a constructive policy. But the 107
minister has gone so far as to say: We are prepared to sit down together and consider the question. That is not a bad policy. Judging from what I can read of the past, good results have followed where men have sat down and joined together and decided on a policy that meant progress for the whple nation. I hope there will be some expression of opinion on this problem, although perhaps not here to-day.	The
leaven is- working and it can be seen in the country; you can see from the press what the people are talking about. They know that we have had too much politics and too much partisanship in the past, and they know that partisanship has not produced very favourable results.	The
Americans, after their experience	with
party Government and partisanship	are
getting rather tired of it. All the evidence goes to show that, in the new time after this war, the only thing possible for a nation is national organization of its resources and its transportation, its educational system, and everything of that kind. A nation will not be in it from this day forth unless -it is nationally organized and unless lit abandons the mistakes that have grown up in the past in dealing with public problems. New times, new methods and nationality must be the governing idea "deling with these great questions. While I throw these statements out, just off the hat as it were, they are convictions that I have reached after careful study of the conditions that have existed here and in other countries. I believe that, if we are to be a nation fit to play our part under the new conditions that will obtain and are already in sight, we shall be able to do it only by listening to such appeals as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) has made to-day and on other occasions. He recently warned us of the danger of the excessive influence of party considerations in the matter of patronage, and a great many other things. We are all to blame for conditions as they exist to-day; both parties are to blame, the public are to blame. But the public expect a change. They expect relief from somebody, or perhaps from some new party that will arise in this country, some new, national party that will have a real national programme and some kind of national leadership, and that will appeal to all the people of Canada for a cessation and abandonment of the present method of working out our problems -and will ap-



proach them on the newer and broader lines which have been indicated here today. The public expect it, and the public will not be satisfied with this Parliament and with our political institutions unless they are modified and changed to some extent, in the direction I have indicated.

With much of what my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) has just said I have a great deal of sympathy. I think that after this war is over we may have less partisanship than we have at present. I am prepared to give my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) this [DOT]much credit, that in many cases what he advocates to-day is the policy of the party in power to-morrow. His policy may not be taken up within a few months or even years, but we have seen the adoption by the party in power of more than one of the principles he has advocated.
The hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce has taken me to task for bringing up the subject of free wheat, and he has said that I have brought it up very often. I can only say to my hon. friend that 1 have not brought it up any oftener thta he has dodged it, for he has dodged it every time it has been brought up. Hearing the Minister of Trade and Commerce speak this afternoon, you would think it was a crime for one of the representatives of a million and a half, or two millions of people, on the prairie, whose principal business it is to grow wheat, who are looking for a market for their wheat to bring this question up, and to bring it up again, in the effort to secure a solution of it. This is a question that it is up to the Government to deal with and it will always be before the Government until it settled. Therefore, no representative of the West is to blame in the slightest degree if he does bring this question up again and again until we get a settlement and a right settlement. My hon. friend makes a statement that is very far from the fact when he says that the freight rate does not affect the farmers in the West, that it does not matter whether the freight is high or low, he gets the same price anyway and that it i3 the consumer across the water who pays the extra freight on the wheat that the farmer grows. I have been a grower of, and a dealer in, wheat in my time and I know that if you are on the market buying wheat at any point on the prairies where wheat is grown, and the freight at Fort William suddenly goes up, we will say from three to

five cents a bushel, just as quickly as the message can be flashed over the wires, down goes the price of wheat to the farmer two cents a bushel. That happens in every case; you cannot get away from it. How is the merchant going to pay the same price for wheat if it costs him two cents a bushel more to send it across from Port Arthur to Montreal? He has to reduce the price paid to the farmer. The freight has everything to do with the price that the farmer gets. Under the present circumstances, occasioned by the war, the freight on wheat across the ocean has gone up from five cents a bushel to 35, 40 and 45 cents. I am not going to be so extreme, or unreasonable, as to claim that if the freight was suddenly brought down to a normal rate the farmer Would get all the advantage of that reduction. I do not think he would under the circumstances, but it certainly would be greatly to his advantage if the rate came down. He would not get it all but he would get part of it. You can. lay it down as a principle which cannot be got over that the cost of freight on wheat between the farm which produces it and the city of Liverpool, or Chicago, or New York, or Minneapolis, or any place where the wheat happens to be sold, is and will always be, one of the most important factors. If my [DOT]hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce says that it makes no difference to the farmer what the rate is, he will find that he has very few followers in the West who will subscribe to his doctrine. During the past ten years there has been a wonderful change .in the knowledge of the farmer on those particular questions relating to the marketing of his crop, to freight rates and everything in connection with the sale of his wheat. He is as well posted in a general way as most men in Canada and just as well posted along the lines of his own business as are other men along the lines of their own particular business.
My hon. friend has dealt at consider-ablfe length, very moderately, with the question of tonnage, but there were two points that my hon. friend avoided, or overlooked, in his discussion that I thought would have had a bearing on the subject and would have been well worthy of mention by my hon. friend. If we are going to secure the building of ships in Canada, would it not	be	well to	put all the
material that goes into the building of these ships on the free list? Would not that be the easiest way to pay a part of the bonus, if a bonus is necessary, to secure the building of ships? Would it not be easier to

simply take the duty off the material that goes into the ships than to pay an extra bonus per ton in connection with the building of ships? There is another factor that would enter very largely into the question of securing tonnage to carry the produce of our farms from this country across the water, and that is the question of securing return freight. If my hon. friend said: We will take off the extra 7J per cent that we put on British goods last year, that would induce trade between Canada and Great Britain, and therefore there would be more tonnage to carry our wheat and other products to the Old Country. It seems to me that that would be a cheaper way of securing tonnage than offering a bonus. If you pay a bonus on tonnage, what will be the result? Take the case of the farmer, and this .applies equally to every man who is a consumer, and we all are consumers. The farmer has to pay the extra duty on goods coming from the Old Country. Then he has, in addition, to pay for the bonus on the building of ships, and in that way he is paying double. In the case of the w-estern farmer, who is refused the right to sell his wheat in the best market, or to have the choice of selling his wheat where the market happens to be best at the time, has to pay three times to secure that extra tonnage. If my hon. friend, instead of just taking off the extra 7J per cent put on last year, w'ould come down with a definite policy, supported by his colleagues, and say that in order to encourage tonnage to come to Canada, and in order to avoid paying a special bonus to secure that tonhage to carry the products of Canada to the Old Country, we will put British goods on the free list-
Would my hon. friend be good enough to say if he would advise anybody to go into the West, settle down and start growing wheat?
If the Government would come forward and say: We will put British goods on the free list-
That is not the point.
Well, then, I misunderstood my hon. friend.
I want to know, with the state of things as it is now, if he would advise people to go into the West and start farming, or chuck the whole thing up?
That is, if goods were put on the free list?
Now, at the present time.

My hon. friend is very
pessimistic. The West is all right.
Answer the question.
I would advise my hon. friend to settle in the West.
What's the trouble?
The trouble is that the Government will not give us the best market for our wheat. My hon. friend would have to work if he came out West, but he is a husky lopking man.

You have knocked
your own case on the head.

I do not wish to be
diverted from my argument. I was saying that if the Minister of Trade a!nd Commerce would put British goods on the free list', there would not be nearly so much difficulty in getting tonnage to carry our products to the Old Country, because that would be an inducement to shipping to come to Canada. If the Government would do that, my hon. friend would not have to ask questions about people going to the West. If people could get their goods right and sell their products in the best market, you could not keep them out of the West with a club. Free wheat does not mean that all our wheat would go to the United States. If the argument of hon. gentlemen is sound, that the Canadian price is better, our wheat would never go to the United States, not one bushel of it. But if we had that extra market, we could take advantage of it exactly as our cattle raisers in the West do. Cattle enter the United States free now, and practically all our cattle are going there, simply because they fetch a higher price than in eastern Canada or across the ocean. Money counts with the farmer when he is selling his cattle, and it would count when he was selling his wheat. If he could get a better price at home he would not sell outside.	.
I entirely agree with the Minister of Trade and Commerce that a country should have a mercantile marine of its own, to carry products to and from the country. The question is, how best to bring that about. I have never been much of an advocate of bonusing industries, but a bonus has this advantage: you know exactly what you are paying. And when it is a question of giving a bonus or putting a duty on an article that is produced in Canada I prefer the bonus, simply because it is more easy

to regulate, and everybody knows exactly what is being paid. But I do not know that a bonus is the best way to secure a mercantile marine. It may be; I do not profess to know very much about this subject; but I think it rather unreasonable for the minister to come here without any proposition whatever to offer to the committee, and then ask my hon. friend from St. John to outline his proposal. Let the minister work out a proposition that will receive the assent of his colleagues first of all, and then submit it to the House, and if it is reasonable I am sure it will receive considerable support from this side of the House. But I do not think it is up to the Opposition to work out a plan for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I do not say that we should not be able to satisfy him, because I have a pretty good opinion of his reasonableness-a much better opinion than I have of the Government as a whole. But while the minister might agree with a proposition coming from this side of the House, his colleagues might not, and it is for that reason that a proposal of this kind should be put forward by the Government in power, and have behind it the weight of the Cabinet's approval.
I have said what little I wanted to say, and I do not apologize to anybody for (bringing up the question of free wheat. I .-shall bring it up just as often as I think .necessary, and shall keep on doing so until we secure that boon for the western farmers; at would be a boon not only to the West font to the whole of Canada and would hurt nobody. I should like to see the minister take a tour through the West, not meeting out-and-out supporters of the Government in the large cities, but attending a few of the farmers' big conventions, the Grain Growers' and the United Farmers' conven- . tions for instance. Let the minister get their view on the free wheat question, and he will soon find that his colleague the Solicitor General was very far from the mark when he said in the House that he was satisfied that ninety per cent of the agitation for free wheat was political, and the other ten per cent mistaken economics.
