Miscellaneous-to provide for the expenses of commission to prepare plans relating to the cities of Ottawa and Hull-further amount required, $2,800.

Has any definite action been taken following the commission's report on the making of Ottawa and Hull into

a federal district, somewhat on the line of Washington?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is aware that an honorary commission was constituted for the purpose of preparing plans for the beautification and improvement of the cities of Ottawa and Hull. The members of the commission were Sir Herbert Holt, Sir Alexander Lacoste, Mr. Frank Darling, Mr. Home Smith, and the mayors of Ottawa and Hull. They did a great deal of work themselves, especially Mr. Darling, and engaged architects and engineers, and consulted town planners in the United States. After giving the work a great deal of care and attention they presented their report, which I am happy to say has, so far as I can learn, met with the general approval of the cities of Ottawa and Hull. *The report is very comprehensive, and its object is to devise a scheme by which the two municipalities and the Dominion Government, the railways and the public utility companies, may all work together looking to a greater Ottawa and Hull in the future, as the federal capital of Canada. My hon. friend asks what action has been taken. The report has only been recently received. The drawings are on exhibition, and if my hon. friend has not already seen them I would suggest that he take the opportunity, because I am sure he will find them very interesting indeed. After the session is over it is my intention to look into this report very carefully, and go over the ground. My hon. friend is no doubt aware that a committee has been appointed by the city of Ottawa for the purpose of interviewing the Government with a view to giving consideration to the plans. Some large questions were raised in the report, notably the federal administration of the Ottawa district. That is a matter which would have to receive very careful consideration, not only by the Government, but by the other bodies interested. I am unable to say anything further except that I am gratified at the way in which the report has been received, and I am satisfied that if all parties will work together we shall, in the years to come, have a capital which will be a credit, in an artistic sense, to the Dominion. A great deal has been done in the planning of various cities throughout the world, Washington being a conspicuous example of what can be done by working to a plan. In Abraham Lincoln's time Washington was a very insignificant 
city indeed, but to-day it is one of the most striking cities in the world.
And one of the cleanest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Washington, of
course, has a better administration and Washington also had the advantage many years ago of a town planner or architect, and the result is the Washington of today.

And he was a good
Frenchman, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I spoke of the
artistic nature of the plans, and I do not know from whom we would be more likely to obtain artistic plans than from a distinguished representative of the race to which my hon. friend belongs. However, this is a start which has been made by the Government getting a plan to which all parties can work, and I think the result will be good. Personally, I desire to give the matter a great deal of attention.

As a resident of Ottawa, I am pleased to hear that my hon. friend will take some interest in this town planning movement. I have glanced at the report published a few weeks ago and I had occasion to discuss this exhaustive report and plan with one of the leading authorities in the United States who was in Chicago a few weeks ago as one of the guests of the Railway Engineering Association, Mr. Brunner, an architect of the city of New York, anp one of ,the leaders in .the movement for town planning in the United States. At present he is engaged in the town planning movement at Cleveland. Mr. Brunner, who by the way delivered on that evening a very able address on the relative position of engineers and architects, told me that in -his judgment that report was a most remarkable one and that the Government had been very fortunate in securing the services of the gentleman who made the plans.
The allusion I made a moment ago to the engineer who made the plan for the city of Washington came to my mind because we have had lately in Montreal a very distinguished French bishop, Monseigneur L'Enfantj who has preached for several Sundays at Notre Dame church. He is a descendant of Colonel L'Enfant, who at the time of the Revolutionary period settled in the United States. He had come with Rocbamtoeau and Lafayette, and he was selected by the authorities of the new republic to lay out a plan for Washington.

He made the plan; it was accepted, but unfortunately he died very poor. He never received a cent for the work that he did for the Republic, although he might have benefited by the expropriations.
Coming back to Ottawa, I may say to my hon. friend that although the plan of the commission is not yet accepted as decisive and final, it is to be expected that it will be finally accepted. My hon. friend and the Government should insist that the municipal authorities at Ottawa should respect the suggestions which are made in that report. . I brought to the attention of the House the other day the question of the height of the new buildings in Ottawa. In the report it is recommended that the buildings should not exceed HO feet in height, and to please a very enterprising gentleman of this city, the city council or the board of control a few weeks ago altered a resolution which had been adopted a few months before following on the lines of the report that the height of the buildings should not exceed 110 feet, and gave permission to that enterprising citizen to build to a height of 130 feet. Since then I notice that the building license has been withdrawn and that .the city council will not allow any permit to be given for buildings exceeding the' height suggested in the report. The Government, however, should have an understanding with the city of Ottawa that the general features of the plan be accepted as final by the city although the Government is not ready to take action on the report. On the whole, I think the Government are to be congratulated on having obtained such an excellent report on what is destined to be the model capital of a great Dominion.
I suppose then the Government is not considering the suggestion made to them some months ago that the capital might be removed to Winnipeg?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have not had the matter under serious consideration.

Will the minister pardon me if I propose here to ask a question which perhaps would not be raised if this were the only amount in the Supplementary Estimates? I find that the Supplementary Estimates amount to the very considerable sum of $4,485,537. The minister will remember that in his Budget speech he stated that while the Main Estimates showed a proposed expenditure of $189,000,000, yet in
making provision for the coming year he thought that the expenditure would not be over about $160,000,000. I may say to my hon. friend, who was not in the House when I was speaking on the matter, that I took occasion to call the attention of different ministers whose Estimates were under consideration to the assurance which had been given by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, and I was not able to ascertain from any minister except the Minister of Public Works that there would be any substantial reduction in the Estimates of the various departments, and the reduction which the Minister of Public Works stated he would be able to make amounted to only $10,000,000. There is a great difference between $10,000,000 and $29,000,000. The Minister of Finance might now, as we are getting near the end of the session, desire to put himself Tight with the country by telling us how the other $19,000,000 was accounted for.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not admit
the necessity of putting myself right with the country, because I think I am usually in that happy position. I may say to my hon. friend that upon three separate occasions when he was absent from the House, I took up the matter to which he has drawn attention, namely, the difference between the estimated expenditure for the coming year and the Estimates, and I pointed out that there were always lapses in connection with Estimates varying from 5 to 20 per cent, and I gave instances to show that during the years of the late Administration it was a usual occurrence to have five, ten, or fifteen million dollars of Estimates unexpended at the end of the fiscal year. For example, when the present Government took office in 1911, the Estimates amounted to about $158,000,000, but the expenditure for the year was only $135,000,000, a difference of $23,000,000. My hon. friend might say: Why were the Estimates so large if your expenditures were only $135,000,000? One reason was that the Supplementary Estimates were very large. At that time they were looking for an election.
Does that oceount for these?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will not say that. If my hon. friend will look at the Estimates and expenditures for the previous year, and the year before that, he will find a similar condition of affaire, but

not quite such a disparity. My hon. friend, in dealing with the question, said that the Estimates amounted to $189,000,000 and that I estimated the expenditure at $160,000,000, and he asked: Where does the $29,000,000 come in? He assumed, of course inaccurately, that the $29,000,000 represents items that will not be gone on with at all. My hon. friend knows very well that lapses occur. There will be in the Estimates many items that will not be gone on with, but in many cases the work will be gone on with, but the amounts that stand opposite those items in the Estimates will not be completely expended. The result will be that $160,000,000 will be approximately the expenditure for the coming year I desire to put this before my hon. friend because I hold strong views as to what the Government will do in the way <of retrenchment in time o'f war. When this wax broke out, I was very glad that *eve were handling a large programme of public works, because there was a very serious dislocation of business, and when there is a serious dislocation of business it is a great advantage in preventing unemployment that there should be a fair programme of public works under way. That was the condition and therefore we refrained at the outbreak of the war from discontinuing expenditure upon public works. I think that was a proper policy at the time; but during this year and so far as I can see for the year that is to come, because the end of this war is certainly not yet in sight, there will be practically no unemployment in Canada. On the other hand there is a demand for labour skilled and unskilled and that demand is likely to increase. The public expenditures in connection with the) war are large, and therefore there is not the necessity for public expenditures in the interest of employment. When I say public expenditures, I mean, of course, useful public expenditures. Therefore the policy which has been laid down by the Government and to which I have referred in the last two Budget speeches is, that while we should go on with works that are under contract, we should not proceed with new works unless such new works are indispensable in the public interest. In a country such as this there are always works which are necessary in the public interest. For example, take the elevators to which my hon.Nfriend sometimes refers. In connection with the grain business, the movement and the storage of the grain, expenditures have to be made for elevator accommo-
dation. Expenditures have to be made on the Intercolonial for rolling stock and expenditures have to be made at various points in Canada for purposes more or less immediately connected with the war. Those expenditures we are making, but a number of expenditures which will be made for public works in times of peace are not being made during the war. There are many items in the Estimates which have been voted-some of them for two years- that will stand in abeyance in the meantime. If the war should come to an end, and if the financial situation and the economic conditions were such that we should feel justified and warranted in proceeding with those expenditures, why, of course, I think it would be proper for us to do so, but as I have stated they will stand in abeyance in the meantime.
Just to show in a word the position for the coming year, because it is a matter which daily engages my attention, I being more intimately connected with the question of providing money than an/ other, I may say that whereas two years ago, that is to say for the fiscal year, 1914-15, our expenditures were about	$187,090,090,
for the coming year our .expenditures will be $160,000,000, as my hon. friend has stated. There is a difference there of some $27,000,000. But included in the expenditures for the coming year is a very large item representing interest on our increased debt. Two years ago the interest charges upon the debt of Canada were about $14,000,000 or $15,000,000, but this year's Estimates include an item for interest of $37,000,000, a difference of some $23,000,000. Then there iwill 'be the outlay for pensions. When my hon. friend takes into consideration the fact that the $160,000,000 includes some $25,000,600 of expenditure necessitated by increase in the public debt and by expenditures on pension account, he will see that the comparison is really between $135,000,000 of expenditure for the coming year and $187,000,000 for two years ago. I may say that that $135,000,000 is about the same as the expenditure for 1911, notwithstanding that our trade this year is the greatest by far in the history of Canada, amounting to some $1,400,000,000. So, I think it goes without saying that the Government is exercising every possible economy. We realize the burden of the war and that that burden ^ill increase- that it will be heavier six months hence than it is to-day, and probably heavier next year than this year. Therefore we are

on common ground in desiring to keep down our expenditures. But it has seemed to me unwise for us (as I stated, my hon. friend not being in the House at the time) to discontinue work upon, let us say, the Quebec bridge. There would, of course, be great loss in connection with such a structure partially completed, and the plant is on t'he spot. Then, the Welland canal work is under contract. The general estimates are less this year than last, 'and we are doing all we can to keep down expenditures, But I do not think it would command public approval if we were to discontinue expenditure on such works as I have mentioned. In the same way the National Transcontinental railway had to be completed, otherwise there would have been great loss. My hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) frequently brings to attention the necessities of St. John, in which he is* interested. I have always observed that he is a great advocate of economy in the abstract, but when it comes to the concrete he will always bring before the House expenditures which he thinks ought to be made. Now, with regard to the Supplementary Estimates for 1915-16 to which we have called attention, they are very moderate, $4,485,000.
Can the minister give us any idea how much the Supplementary Estimates for next year will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot say offhand, but I think they are comparatively small because we are pursuing the policy I have indicated. In connection with the Supplementary Estimates for 1915-16, now before us, my hon. friend will observe that there are several large items. For instance, there is the relief for seed grain, $1,550,000. That has already been provided for by Governor General's warrants, and this Estimate is not strictly or legally necessary, because a Governor General's warrant is a perfectly legitimate means of providing funds. But I thought it well-and it is an innovation-to include in the Estimates amounts raised by Governor General's warrants in order that the House may have before it the total expenditures made. Then we have a further item for working expenses of the Intercolonial amounting to $1,500-
000.	The scope of the operations of the Intercolonial has been largely increased by the war. On the other side of the Intercolonial account will be found a very gratifying increase in earnings, in fact I have be$n surprised and much gratified
that the earnings have been so large within the last year or so. So, this amount is by no means wasted but is a necessary expenditure in connection with the Government road. Having regard to all the considerations I have mentioned, I am sure that my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), with his usual fair-mindedness, will agree that he has been entirely mistaken as to the Government pursuing a policy that even savours of extravagance, and that we have exercised the most rigid economy since the outbreak of the war. The hon. gentleman himself has been a Minister of Public Works, and looking over the Estimates that he presented to the House in the past, as I have done, I have never found any evidence of that economical spirit which he now exhibits from time to time. But I do not charge that against him, for this is war time and I quite agree with what I conceive to be his view, that in war time, so far as the ordinary expenditures of the country are concerned, it is the duty of the Government to exercise all possible economy consistently with carrying on the business of the country. But there is a point beyond which if you carry economy you become parsimonious and the public interest undoubtedly suffers. There is another feature which I touched upon on one or two occasions in the House, and it is this:
It must not be assumed that while the war is on, the expenditures of departments of Government other than the Militia Department, which, of course, is immediately concerned with the war, will if an economical policy is- observed, be necessarily less than they would be in times of peace. My experience has been that in nearly all departments since the war broke out there is an added burden by reason of the war. Take the Customs Department, for example. In connection with the collection of revenue and with the embargo upon various classes of goods and commodities much additional work is entailed. A great deal of additional work has been thrown upon the Commissioner of Customs; I was talking to him about it yesterday. In other departments, my own, for example, the work has increased very greatly and the expenditure has increased correspondingly. Men are working day and night at the same salary that they received before-working uncomplainingly and zealously in the interests of the department, of the Government and of the country at this time. Nearly all the

staffs are increased. We have endeavoured, so far as we have been able to do so consistently with proper administration of the public business, to cut down our ordinary and capital expenditures since the outbreak of the war.

The reference which the Minister of Finance has made to the necessity for building elevators to give aceommo-dation for grain even during war times is an unfortunate one. It happens that in connection with the whole system of Government railways there is only one small elevator with a capacity of 750,000 bushels, and this Government apparently has given no thought to the matter of providing increased storage accommodation in connection with the Intercolonial railway or the Transcontinental railway, which the Government is operating. At the port of St. John, one of the two chief winter ports of Canada, where the grain elevator formerly operated in connection with the Intercolonial railway .was burned down some two years ago, no step has been taken to build a new elevator. I say that this reference of my hon. friend was unfortunate, because his colleague the Acting Minister of Railways Tather sought to make the excuse that while the war is on he did not think it desirable to rebuild the elevator, though he said that as soon as possible after the war is over steps would be taken to that end. My hon. friend says that in the year 1911, during part of which the Liberal Government was in power, the actual expenditure was $135,000,000. That included, he says very truly, all the expenditures in connection with the items that were contained in the Supplementary Estimates of that year, which , were, as he says, pretty large, as well as those in the main Estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend misunderstood me. I did not say that the $135,000,000 included the items in the Estimates. I said that the Estimates, including the Supplementaries, were $158,000,000.

And the expenditure was $135,000,000. My hon. friend said that the total Estimates, main and supplementary, amounted to $158,000,000, while the actual expenditure was $135,000,000. These were times of peace, plenty and prosperity. This Government came into power towards the middle of that fiscal year, when prosperity was abounding in the country. The reflex action had not taken place. There was every reason why the Government should go on

with all necessary public works. For the coming year, notwithstanding the dreadful condition of distress which prevails throughout this country, affecting practically all classes of people except those engaged in the manufacture of munitions of war, this Government comes down with main Estimates to the amount of $189,000,000, or $53,000,000 more than was expended out of main and supplementary Estimates in 1911. That is an enormous increase; it is double the total revenues of Canada at the time of Confederation. The minister has not come down with his supplementaries; he says they will be comparatively small. If he means that relatively to the Estimates of this year, they will be comparatively small, certainly they will run up to quite a number of millions of dollars, and to the $189,000,000 would have to be added the total amount contained in the supplementary Estimates. I am a little suspicious, if the minister will pardon my saying so, when the minister cannot tell us what his Supplementary Estimates for the current year will be. He must have given them very careful consideration by this time, because if it had not been for certain unexpected disclosures and for certain demands by various railway companies, prorogation would probably have taken place before Easter. When the minister at this late date in the session cannot tell what the Supplementary Estimates will amount to, it gives rise to the suspicion that they will be considerably larger than he would like to let the committee know at this time. The hop. gentleman spoke of myself when I was Minister of Public Works; he is not able to see, in looking back over the Estimates, that I was very economical. At that time my hon. friend belonged to a party that was economical; therefore he would view my Estimates through the glasses of economy. But if he would look at them to-day he would find them very economical as compared with the expenditures of his colleague, the present Minister of Public Works. The total expenditures of the Department of Public Works during the last three years of the late Government were only about $37,000,000 as against a little over $80,000,000 during the first three years that the present Minister of Public Works, had full charge of that department. What, does the minister think of that? He says that I was very extravagant. What does he think of the action of the present Government in expending in the Department of Public Works during a certain period two

and a half times as much as was expended during a similar period when I had the honour of having charge of the department? My hon. friend says that this Government has not gone on and made any great increases in expenditures, notwithstanding the fact that the trade of Canada amounted to $1,400,000,000. Does the minister put the enormous amount of that trade forward as a reason why the Government would have been justified in going on with great expenditures, just as if these were glorious times of peace and as if that trade was the result of peaceful development of the country? Surely not. Does not the minister know that the enormous trade of $1,400,000,000 is the result of war conditions? Does he not know that it is the result of the enormous demand for clothing, provisions, and all kinds of supplies needed at the front? Does he not know that included in that are the supplies sent forward by this Government to supply our own men? That they all go in and fill up the total amount of the trade of this country? Does he not know that all the money that comes in in payment for the manufacture of many of these war supplies and so on, not only for our own men but for the Allies, goes to swell up the imports, and' that these altogether make up this $1,400,000,000 ? Much of that trade' results from unfortunate circumstances of which no Government ought to be proud, and by which no Government ought to be made happy. Yet the minister at times cannot help boasting of this enormous increase of trade, and he takes it as an evidence of proper and legitimate and desirable prosperity on the part of the people of this country. That very condition, the fact that we are sending away, for the use of our men at the front, these vast quantities of goods, ought to be an incentive to greater economy. The fact that we have before us the evidence of the ravages which this war is making, not only upon the Allies but upon Canada, the way in which it is sapping the energies and taking away the prosperity of the people, ought to make us more economical than if there was no war. I hope the minister will not talk any more about the economy of this Government. Think, with 8,000,000 of people this Government is coming down with a proposed expenditure of $189,000,000! I have asked the minister' how he accounted for the $29,000,000 difference. We have asked every minister whose Estimates have been before
us, even the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals, and with one accord, with one voice, they all, in effect, said that the Minister of Finance did not know what he was talking about, that they were going to expend practically every dollar contained in the Estimates of their different departments. That is why I call the attention . of the Minister of Finance to the fact that he is $19,000,000 out of the way, according to the evidence which we have before us from the various ministers whose Estimates have been discussed. The only min- 1 ister who gave us the slightest aid, who sought to bolster up the credit or reliability of the Minister of Finance, was the Minister of Public Works, and to the extent of $10,000,000 he acted like a man, he stood right at the back of the Minister of Finance. But every other minister went back on him with the exception of the Minister of Marine, who threw off about $5,000.
Royal Mint-further amount required, $13,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Royal Mint has had a great deal of additional work thrown on it this year for the Imperial Government. I am not at liberty to give details, but of course any expenditure which we make will be returned in the charges which are made by the Mint for their services.
Unforeseen expenses, expenditure thereof to be under Order In Council, and a detailed statement to be laid before Parliament within fifteen days of next session, $40,000.
Do we get that statement always?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, within fifteen days after the opening of each session a statement of the unforeseen expenditure item is laid on the table.
Grant to the National Battlefields Commission-
(a)	For expenses of administration, $7,200.
(b)	For maintenance of the National Battlefields Park, $26,560.
(c)	For maintenance of Martello tower No. 4, $400.

Could the minister tell us anything about that Battlefields Commission? My right hon, friend the leader of the Opposition takes a great deal of interest in it and usually asks a series of questions about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This year I asked them to confine their expenditure practically to maintenance. There is really no new work being carried on. They have cut down their Estimate.
There is an increase of $11,560 over last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was another item in last year. Their Estimate is undoubtedly out down. It ran as high as $100,000. The total amount for this year is about $37,000. There must be some item left out, or not embraced in a, b and e, because, as I have said, they are keeping their expenditure down to a maintenance basis. When the war broke out I asked them to go slow on that work.
But you have an increase of $11,560.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is some item that is not mentioned in the Estimates for this year. But if my hon. friend is interested especially in the matter I will be glad to allow the item to stand and get a full explanation. It is much less than last year.

I would like to have it stand that the leader of the Opposition may have a dhance to say something in regard to it. He may not want to make any comments on it, but he takes a deep interest in it, and it is one of the items that he probably will have something to say upon. I will call his attention to it in the morning, and if he does not wish to have any discussion upon it I will tell my hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) and he can bring it up and put it through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Very good.
Grant to the Medical Council of Canada, $15,000.
Mr. PUGrSLEY: How is ihat expended?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is paid over to, and expended for the purposes of, the Council. This grant dates back two or three years. At that time they were considering the . matter of a uniform qualification for physicians throughout Canada. I made inquiry and I found that it is entirely required for the purposes of the Council. There may come a time when it will not be required, or when so much will not be required, but it seems to be necessary now.
Contribution to aid in carrying on the work of the Astronomical Society of Canada, $2,000.
I think that might very well be dropped this year. It is not large, but what is the urgency of it during war time ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend has nothing of the Philistine in him, and,

after all, we must continue to assist some of these societies. It is a very small grant and for a very worthy object.
Royal Academy of Arts, $5,000.
How is this expended?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By the Academy for the promotion of its objects. It is the annual grant which has been made for years past.
Where are the headquarters of the Academy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think in Montreal, 'but if my hon. friend is interested I will allow the matter to stand and get full information.

I might tell my hon. friend why I am interested. I find here a great many items of a miscellaneous character which could all stand over, or all be omitted, without the slightest injury to the public service. I do think that in these war times they ought to be allowed to stand. Take the grant to the Medieal Council as an illustration and which amounts to $15,000; the minister cannot tell the committee what is done with that. Surely if that grant is made just to pay the expenses of a meeting They might defer their meeting for one year or until the war is over.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is for examinations.
The medical councils of the different provinces carry on the examinations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But this is for the whole Dominion and for all the provinces.

It would not take anything like $15,000 to pay the expenses. Then take these other societies-the Astronomical Society, and the Royal Academy oft Arte; these items could stand over without the slightest injury to the public service. They all run up to a large sum. We have to take some action in reference to these items. We may offend somebody by doing so but it is our duty. It is not a matter of $2,000, or $5,000 or $15,000, but it runs into hundreds of thousands of dollars and if the minister would look these items over carefully he can see where a saving of hundreds of thousands of dollars can be made. These amounts have nothing to do with public works, they have nothing

to -do with ordinary labouring people who need employment but they are largely for scientific and social purposes. They are on a par with the $100,000 which was voted for the Geodetic surveys and which are no more needed to be kept there than a horse requires to have five legs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Carried.
"Carried," says the minister. No effect on the Minister of Finance at all. Can he not find his way to moving to strike some of these items out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot believe my hon. friend is serious, because he is an . intellectual man and should have sympathy with these scientific objects. It is not only the tangible and material that we should be interested in, but we should not lose interest in science, literature and art even though war is on.
.Contribution to McGill University towards the maintenance of a Regional Bureau for Canada, for the International Catalogue of Scientific Literature, $2,000.

What is the object of
this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This grant has been in the Estimates for some years. My hon. friend can understand the importance of having these scientific publications properly catalogued.
Grant towards the erection of a monument to Samuel de Champlain at Orillia, Ont., revote $7,500.	' j'	. y 4ti

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This monument
has been in the hands of the statuaries for some time, and the $7,500 will be required almost immediately to pay for the work. The item might have stood over had the work not been commenced.
Towards meeting any d flc'ency arising in connection with the election of the Champlain monument, Ottawa, $3,000.

What is the obligation
with respect to this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is in connection with the monument at Nepean Point. The Dominion Government made a grant towards that monument, and there were also a number of private subscriptions, but on account of the war a certain number of these subscriptions could not be collected. They were all made in good faith, and would have been paid but for the war. A year ago it looked as if we should have to put in a much larger item than this $3,000, but since then some contributions that were not expected have come in, making the deficit now about $3,000.
I suppose it goes to the sculptor?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not quite
sure, but if it does, it is serving a very worthy purpose, for the sculptor must be paid.

I think for the peace,
harmony and good-will of the Minister of Finance and his successor, the different bodies that get these grants, small though they be, should send informa-
II p.m. tion with respect to them to the Minister of Finance. He is compelled to handle these Estimates in the House, but is afforded little or no information with respect to them. Doubtless when the grants were originally made there were good reasons for them, and the reasons were given. I think the different associations should be asked to send in a memorandum of what they do with the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think there is a good deal in what my hon. friend says. These applications for grants are looked into very carefully by my deputy, and we receive, I suppose, about twice as many applications as appear here. The one that appear in the Estimates are those about which no question arises, the different bodies doing good work and being altogether worthy. I am inclined to think that the information my hon. friend has in mind is in the department, but of course neither I nor any other minister would carry these details in his head, knowing that if any serious question arose about them in committee the information could be obtained from the department.
Progress reported.
On motion of Sir Thomas White, the House adjourned at 11.08 p.m.
Thursday, April 27, 1916.
